title: What Causes Flight Delays?
text:
OverviewDeparture TimeDelay DistributionInteractive GameAbout the Data



How Often Are Flights Delayed?
Across all 328,521 departed flights from New York City (JFK, LGA, EWR) in 2013, the majority left on schedule:

  
    
      On-Time / Early
      60.9%
      200,089 flights (≤ 0 min)
    
  
  
    
      Minor Delay
      17.6%
      57,658 flights (1–15 min)
    
  
  
    
      FAA Delayed
      21.5%
      70,774 flights (> 15 min)
    
  
  
    
      Severe Delay
      8.1%
      26,581 flights (> 60 min)
    
  


60.9% departed early or on the exact minute.
17.6% experienced minor delays under 15 minutes, which airlines still classify as “on-time” under standard aviation metrics.
21.5% were officially delayed by more than 15 minutes.
8.1% suffered major disruptions exceeding an hour.




What Actually Causes Flight Delays?
Flight delays are rarely isolated events. According to official records from the Bureau of Transportation Statistics (BTS) and Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), the most common drivers of flight delays are:

1. Late-Arriving Aircraft (~38% of all delay minutes)

The “Domino Effect”: Commercial aircraft fly multiple legs per day. When a morning flight into New York arrives 45 minutes late, its afternoon departure is automatically delayed, carrying the delay across the entire network.

2. Air Carrier Operations (~30% of delay minutes)

Issues directly under the airline’s management, including mechanical maintenance checks, crew duty-hour limits, baggage loading bottlenecks, and aircraft cleaning/fueling turnaround times.

3. National Aviation System & Airspace Congestion (~24% of delay minutes)

Heavy air traffic volume requiring air traffic control (ATC) spacing, runway congestion at peak travel hours, and airport ground stops. NYC airports are among the most congested in the nation.

4. Severe Weather (~7% of delay minutes)

Extreme conditions such as thunderstorms, snow blizzards, heavy fog, and high wind shears that halt takeoffs or close flight corridors for passenger safety.

5. Security Breaches (<1% of delay minutes)

Rare terminal re-screenings or security perimeter incidents.





Each dot below represents one flight with a recorded departure delay. The horizontal axis is its scheduled departure time; the vertical axis is how many minutes early or late it actually departed. The view is zoomed to delays between 30 minutes early and 3 hours late to show the primary cluster.


Code
flights |>
  filter(!is.na(dep_delay)) |>
  mutate(
    scheduled_hour = sched_dep_time %/% 100 +
      (sched_dep_time %% 100) / 60
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = scheduled_hour, y = dep_delay)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.08, size = 0.35, color = "#176B87") +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(0, 24, by = 3),
    limits = c(0, 24),
    labels = \(x) sprintf("%02d:00", x)
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-30, 180)) +
  labs(
    x = "Scheduled departure time",
    y = "Departure delay (minutes)",
    caption = "Flights with missing departure-delay values are omitted."
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








Figure 1: Each point is a flight; the y-axis is zoomed to show the main cluster.






Key Takeaways from the Scatter Plot

Early morning flights are most reliable: Flights scheduled between 5:00 AM and 8:00 AM cluster tightly near zero delay.
Delays build throughout the day: As planes fly multiple legs, earlier delays propagate, creating a taller spread of delays in the afternoon and evening.
Many flights depart early: Negative delay values (below 0) represent flights leaving up to 15–30 minutes ahead of schedule.
Extreme delays concentrate late: Delays exceeding 2 hours become noticeably more frequent after 3:00 PM.




This histogram summarizes flight records into 5-minute bins. The bar heights show how many flights fell into each delay range, and the red dashed line marks the 15-minute delay mark.


Code
flights |>
  filter(!is.na(dep_delay)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = dep_delay)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, fill = "#176B87", color = "white") +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = 15,
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "#C4492D",
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-30, 180)) +
  labs(
    x = "Departure delay (minutes; early departures are negative)",
    y = "Number of flights",
    caption = "The x-axis is zoomed to −30 to 180 minutes; the dashed line is 15 minutes late."
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)








Figure 2: Departure-delay counts for 328,521 flights with recorded values.






Key Takeaways from the Histogram

Strong peak near zero: The single most common outcome is departing right on time or within 5 minutes of schedule.
Most flights leave on time: Out of 328,521 flights, 200,089 (about 61%) left on time or early.
The 15-minute threshold: Under FAA standards, flights delayed under 15 minutes are considered on-time. Only 70,774 flights (about 21.5%) were officially delayed.
Right-skewed distribution: Long delays decrease sharply in frequency—delays over 2 hours are relatively rare compared to small delays.




Test your intuition! Can you guess whether a flight was delayed based on its departure airport, time, and carrier?

The data come from the nycflights13 R package. Each row represents a scheduled flight from JFK, LGA, or EWR in 2013. Missing departure delays generally correspond to flights that did not depart, so the charts describe flights with an observed departure—not cancellations.
